title: Post-Course Portfolio: Online Multiplayer Game Platform
descriptionMarkdown:
# Online Multiplayer Game Platform

## Position in the curriculum
Post-course portfolio expansion, and the hardest entry in the catalog: build this last, after the Real-Time Tic-Tac-Toe or Connect Four/Battleship project (for the core game-session pattern), the Authentication & User Management System (for real accounts), and the Real-Time Chat Application (for authenticated, persisted, room-scoped WebSocket messaging). This project is a generalization of all three, not a fourth unrelated game.

## Beyond what the lessons taught
This project assumes all the WebSocket and authentication research already done for the earlier real-time catalog entries. Matchmaking queue design and horizontal scaling of stateful WebSocket sessions across multiple server instances are genuinely advanced topics with no single canonical lesson; treat them as open-ended research, and it is entirely acceptable to scope this project to a single server instance (documenting that limitation explicitly) rather than attempting real multi-instance scaling.

## Already-proven foundation
This project's "game room" abstraction should be built to host more than one previously-built game (reuse your Tic-Tac-Toe and/or Connect Four session logic behind a common `GameSession` interface, per Chapter 20's architecture discipline), rather than building a fourth game engine from scratch — the platform, not any single game, is the point.

## Project scope
Authenticated players join a matchmaking queue for a chosen game type; once two (or more, depending on the game) compatible players are queued, the platform creates a game room and hands off to that game's own session logic, exactly as in the earlier real-time projects. Track and persist per-player statistics (games played, won, lost) updated transactionally at game end. Add a lobby view (a REST endpoint, not WebSocket) listing currently open/joinable rooms for spectating or joining, and handle a player disconnecting mid-match by applying that game's own documented disconnect policy from the earlier project it was built in. Explicitly document your concurrency model for the matchmaking queue itself: two players joining the queue at nearly the same instant must be matched together exactly once, never matched into two different games simultaneously.

## Required evidence
- A matchmaking concurrency test firing several near-simultaneous join requests and confirming every player is matched into exactly one room, with no player left in two rooms or none.
- A test confirming per-player statistics update transactionally and correctly at game end, including a test of what happens to statistics when a match ends by disconnect/forfeit rather than a normal win.
- A test demonstrating at least two different game types running through the same `GameSession` abstraction, proving the platform layer is genuinely game-agnostic.
- A documented, explicit statement of this project's scaling limitations (single-instance, in-memory session state, or whatever you chose) rather than an implied claim of production-grade horizontal scalability.
- A lobby-listing test confirming a room disappears from the joinable list once it is full or completed.

## Review and completion
A reviewer queues four players for two different game types at nearly the same time, expects two correctly-matched games to start (one per game type, two players each), then has one player in one game disconnect and asks you to demonstrate the documented disconnect policy actually firing, and finally asks you to name, precisely, what would have to change for this platform to run correctly across more than one server instance — an honest answer, not a claim that it already does.
learningObjectives: Generalize two or more previously-built game sessions behind one common platform abstraction
Design and test a matchmaking queue's concurrency guarantees under simultaneous join attempts
Update per-player statistics transactionally and correctly for both normal and disconnect-ended matches
Separate a game-agnostic platform layer from game-specific session logic, per the architecture chapter's boundary discipline
State a project's real scaling limitations honestly rather than implying untested production-readiness
